topics.label: Lecture introduction and framing
topics.groupedBecause: This opening frames the lecture as an integration of previously introduced immune cells and molecules.

topics.label: Principles of innate immune recognition
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how inherited, appropriately located receptors distinguish microbial products and tissue damage from normal host components.

topics.label: Toll-like receptor recognition and signalling
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how toll-like receptors translate microbial recognition into responses suited to the location of the infection.

topics.label: Other pattern recognition receptors and inflammasome activation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how danger-sensing pathways beyond toll-like receptors activate inflammation and can contribute to inflammatory disease.

topics.label: Sentinel-cell activation and leukocyte recruitment
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how activated sentinel cells initiate an inflammatory response that brings circulating leukocytes to the infection site.

topics.label: Lymphatic transport and adaptive immune priming
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how dendritic cells carry evidence of tissue infection through lymphatic drainage to initiate adaptive responses in lymph nodes.

topics.label: Excessive systemic inflammation and septic shock
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic examines how excessive inflammatory activation becomes a life-threatening systemic response.

topics.label: Passive and active resolution of inflammation
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how inflammatory activity subsides through loss of activating stimuli and increasing inhibitory signals.

topics.label: Tissue repair and persistent inflammation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine why recovery from tissue damage may leave persistent inflammation, including containment of infections that cannot be cleared.

topics.label: Lecture close and next lecture
topics.groupedBecause: This closing ends the lecture and identifies complement as the subject of the next lecture.
